figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1. Learning to Theorize (L2T) Framework. (a) Training data consists of observation pairs (x, y) generated by unobserved true programs. (b) Under L2T, the model learns to discover reusable primitives (Rotate, Left, Down, and Paint) and to compose them into executable theories. (c) Without L2T, the model instead memorizes entangled composite primitives (e.g., Left-Down) as indecomposed single units. (d) Once the model has learned to theorize, novel phenomena (e.g., Down-Paint-Rotate) can be explained by recombining learned primitives. (e) In contrast, memorized entangled representations fail to generalize to unseen programs.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2. Computation graph of Neural Theorizer (NEO). NEO infers a latent program by iteratively selecting a primitive z_ik with the theory programmer q_phi(z_ik | s_k, y) and executing it via the transition model p_theta(s_{k+1} | s_k, z_ik). Each intermediate state s_k is decoded into a full reconstruction y_hat_k = D_theta(s_k); through state grounding (Sec. 3.4), these intermediate predictions are explicitly regularized to remain valid observations, preventing degenerate or blurry intermediate states. The MDL criterion selects the shortest accurate explanation length k* (green), which in turn provides a learning signal that favors short yet accurate program compositions (Sec. 3.3).

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4. Visualization of explanations for a compositional OOD in the image-editing task (α = 0.66). The leftmost column shows the observed source–target pair (x, y). Baseline models generate y via a single-step prediction or by relying on action combinations observed only in the in-distribution data, and thus fail to decompose the novel OOD transformation. In contrast, NEO explains the same phenomenon as a sequence of learned primitive actions, enabling systematic OOD generalization through explicit compositional explanations.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 frames theory-building against entangled prediction; Figure 2 instantiates NEO’s programmer–transition–grounding–MDL loop; Tables 1–2 establish GridWorld/Arithmetic transfer and Figure 3 supplies Image Editing comparison. Figures 4–5 turn the result into qualitative explanation and adaptive length, Figure 6 links sampling to execution paths, and Figure 7 measures primitive coverage. Appendix Figure 8 and Table 3 probe MDL/grounding, Figures 9–18 decompose code alignment across domains, Figures 19–20 quantify test-time scaling, Figures 21–22 show long-horizon rollouts, and Tables 4–27 expose definitions, splits, cost, data scale and hyperparameters.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Captions start with a numbered label and usually combine a setting, comparison/encoding key and conclusion. Figures 1–6 are relatively self-contained and often state the main finding; Figures 8–19 and 21–22 are terse and rely on nearby appendix prose. Result-table captions define three-run means and NEO-S budgets, while split/configuration tables identify their scope but rarely include counts or missingness conventions.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Performance Tables 1–3 and 11 use repeated alpha row groups and two-level condition headers: In-distribution, Comp. OOD and Length OOD each split into Self-Ex./Transf. Definition/split tables use compact Primitive/Description or Split/Category/Combinations columns; cost/data tables name units and OOD counts explicitly; hyperparameter tables use stable Hyperparameter/Value or four-method columns with italic section rows.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figure 2’s computation graph predicts adaptive primitive sequences; Tables 1–2 and Figure 3 test transfer, Figure 4 visualizes a decomposed OOD instance, and Figure 5 shows MDL stopping. Table 3 and Figure 8 intervene on grounding, codebook capacity and lambda_MDL; Figures 9–18 localize primitive/composite assignments; Figures 6, 19–20 and Tables 12–14 measure sampling and cost; Figures 21–22 expose the remaining long-horizon failure mode.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: The seven main figures and three main tables establish the concept, method and cross-domain result. Appendix objects preserve the exact primitive/split vocabulary (Tables 4–10), expand Image Editing and alignment (Table 11, Figures 9–18), separate test-time scaling and qualitative paths (Figures 19–22), and make cost, dataset size and hyperparameters inspectable (Tables 12–27).
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Native text and tables use Nimbus Roman/Computer Modern math, while imported plot/diagram labels mix DejaVu Sans, Aptos/Calibri and monospaced code labels. Main diagram and chart labels are mostly 6–10 pt; heatmap tick labels, qualitative operators and appendix configuration cells are at the lower legibility edge. Table typography is more stable than figure typography because it remains native PDF text.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Blue consistently identifies NEO or high-count heatmap cells, gray identifies monolithic baselines/GT, and light-blue row shading identifies proposed methods in performance tables. Saturated orange/red/green/yellow tile colors represent qualitative operators, while solid/dashed edge styles add path identity in Figure 22. The palette is semantically coherent but not fully colorblind/grayscale robust.

most_reusable_patterns: Lead with a conceptual failure/success contrast, then place a method computation graph immediately before the first quantitative transfer tables.
Reuse one two-level alpha × condition × metric table grammar across domains, with NEO row shading and exact three-run means.
Pair aggregate OOD performance with a selected primitive-chain montage and a training/MDL or code-alignment diagnostic.
Keep codebook alignment matrices on a shared row/column order across alpha and lambda settings so entanglement changes remain visually attributable.
Separate test-time scaling curves, compute tables and qualitative execution graphs so accuracy, cost and search mechanism are all visible.
failure_patterns: Many figures and tables report point means or illustrative traces without a displayed dispersion definition, denominator or seed-level values.
Heatmaps, small-multiple scaling panels and hyperparameter tables are information-dense; tiny labels and repeated legends weaken print-scale auditability.
Color is often the primary method or state channel; blue/gray quantitative plots are partly redundant, but qualitative tiles and heatmaps are not grayscale-safe.
Several appendix captions are too terse to define matching denominators, unavailable cells or band statistics without adjacent prose.
The public author repository supplies rendered PNG/GIF cross-checks but no editable plot/table/LaTeX generator, preventing source-exact parameter recovery.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: The paper uses a theory-first visual system—conceptual contrast, NEO computation graph, cross-domain transfer tables, OOD montages, MDL/alignment diagnostics and test-time scaling—to make reusable latent programs inspectable, while uncertainty metadata, dense appendix typography and the lack of editable public visual sources limit full reproducibility.
